The deadlock affecting the current package is no longer an isolated procedural hiccup. Nigeria proposes that paragraphs 124 to 129 of note S/2024/507 be modified to include a default mechanism, one that allows outstanding positions to be filled by rotation among eligible candidates from the relevant regional group on an interim basis where consensus on the package is not reached within 60 days of the start of the Council's year. A subsidiary body should not go without leadership because a wider membership cannot agree on a package deal that has nothing to do with the mandate of that body. Second, on Rule 37 and Rule 39, in practice, participation by specially affected states still depends on case-by-case accommodation rather than clear entitlement. Nigeria proposes that the Council adopt defined criteria under which a state qualifies as specially affected, including states named in the resolution under discussion, neighboring states to an active conflict, and troop and police contributing countries to relevant mission, and that participation under Rule 37 be presumptive once those criteria are met, rather than a matter of individual request and Council's discretion. Third, on pen holding, African situations continue to occupy a large share of the council's agenda. Nigeria proposes that co-pen holding with the elected African members on African file items becomes the default arrangement, not the exception. President, the Council will soon conduct its second straw poll related to the selection and appointment of the next Secretary-General. We call on the Council to share the outcomes of such straw polls, as we heard from the briefers this morning as well, and to do so formally with all Member States to ensure transparency and inclusivity, not merely to inform it that a poll has taken place. While we acknowledge improvements in the selection process of the Secretary-General in line with UN General Assembly Resolution 79/327, we also call for transparency in the selection process by the Council prior to the submission of its recommendations to the General Assembly. To give effect to the latter, if the Council is unable to make a single recommendation, it should consider recommending more than one candidate for the General Assembly to decide, on and to exercise its due authority on the matter. President, we also encourage meaningful consultations with member states on the agenda of the Security Council. In recent years, the council's functioning has improved with greater role played by the elected members on the council. This includes a more active role of these members based on their respective comparative expertise and advantages as pen holders for resolutions and various outcomes of the council. We appreciate that the African members of the Council, the A3, have been afforded a greater role in this regard, especially in terms of matters impacting the African continent. We welcome the continued engagement between the Peace and Security Council of the African Union and the UN Security Council to further synergize efforts to bring about lasting peace through the permanent silencing of the guns in Africa. In this regard, we look forward to the review of the Security Council Resolution 2719 and its implementation by the Council in support of African-led peacekeeping operations. President, we have noted with appreciation the efforts undertaken for informal engagement on the annual report of the Council and encourages the continuation of this practice for engagement with the wider UN membership. In this regard, we underscore the need for substantive and substantial annual reports rather than a mere narrative on the activities undertaken by the Council. In conclusion, Mr. President, pending the indispensable structural reform of the UN Security Council, there is much that can be done by the Council to improve its working methods to ensure that it is able to respond to pressing and urgent international peace and security challenges. It has been the elected members of the Council that have led the work in this respect. drawing on Article 24 of the Charter, which provides that the Council members, carrying out their duties under their responsibilities to the Council, act on behalf of all UN Member States. It would be in the best interest of the Council and enhance its integrity if all members of the Council followed this example. I thank you.
I thank the representative of South Africa for the statement, and I now give the floor to the representative of Australia.

Thank you, President. And let me also thank our briefer, Shamila Khandiah-Thomsen, for your contribution today. It's much appreciated. President, the Security Council acts on behalf of all member states in executing its primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security. Working methods, as we're discussing today, matter because they're the means by which the council fulfills that responsibility. We believe that effective, transparent and inclusive ways of working equip the Council to implement its critical mandate. They also allow the wider membership to hold the Council accountable. Australia wishes to make four points. First, we are profoundly concerned by the ongoing delay in appointing chairs of the Council's subsidiary bodies. These bodies undertake much of the essential day-to-day work of the Council and facilitate the provision of valuable information and analysis to all Member States. Regrettably, the delay has deprived all Member States of the full benefit of this important reporting and engagement, and we urge the Council to resolve the current impasse and consider practical options for avoiding similar delays in the future, including by formulating clear written pathways for resolving any disagreements that may arise. Second, The Council is currently engaged in one of its most important tasks, formulating a recommendation to the General Assembly for the appointment of the next Secretary-General. Australia welcomes efforts to make this process more transparent, and it is unfortunate that additional measures could not also be agreed. It will be important to document lessons learnt once the process is complete so that future Council members can benefit from the experience of current members. Third, we reiterate our longstanding concerns regarding the use of the veto, which too often prevents the council from responding meaningfully to crises. We continue to support the ACT code of conduct and the French Mexican initiative. We also urge council members to fully adhere to article 27 three of the charter and support efforts to clarify its provisions. Finally, the conduct of council meetings deserves continued attention. Adherence to speaking time limits by briefers and council members would promote more focused deliberations and help ensure responsible use of limited United Nations resources. President, working methods are more than a technical exercise. They are a critical tool that allows the council to implement its mandate on behalf of the wider membership. And Australia supports a council that is transparent, inclusive, representative, and effective, As candidates for the Council in 2029 and 30, we pledge to work constructively with all Member States to achieve this goal. Thank you.
I thank the representative of Australia for the statement, and I now give the floor to the representative of Spain.

Thank you, Mr President. Thank you for convening this open debate, and since this is the first time that my delegation is taking the floor during your presidency. We are convinced that a Council that is more representative, democratic and transparent is also a more effective organ and better prepared to respond to contemporary challenges of international peace and security. When procedures are inclusive and predictable, legitimacy of the decisions of the council is clearly strengthened. Note S slash 2 2024 slash 507 is a valuable exercise. of consolidation of good practices, which should continue to evolve to respond to the new challenges confronting this Council. For this, it is essential to improve the predictability of the work and timely access to documentation and information. These are essential elements to ensure the inclusivity and effective participation of Member States. The Toledo Formula, introduced by Spain in 2015 during our Presidency of the Council, is a concrete example of how to move in this direction. Wrap-up sessions are not a mere monthly summary, but rather a forum for dialogue, where Permanent Representatives respond to questions. We also believe it's necessary to expand spaces for dialogue and building trust through the more frequent use of informal meetings and interactive dialogues. With regard to the application of rules 37 and 39, Spain attaches great importance to the participation of States especially affected by the issues examined by this Council. Mr. President, to facilitate broader consensus, it's essential to move towards a more balanced distribution of the work of the Council, especially with regard to the distribution of drafting of resolutions. We urge once again all member states to join the Franco-Mexican initiative that promotes the restraint in the use of veto in case of mass atrocities and the code of conduct of the ACT Group, but we believe that both initiatives should be incorporated to the rules of procedure of the Council. We also recall that Article 27.3 of the Charter is applicable to all members of the Council. Mr. President, to conclude, methods of work of the Council must adapt to respond adequately to contemporary realities. Our common objective should be to make sure that the provision, these provisions lead to tangible practices and results that strengthen the legitimacy and the effectiveness of the Security Council. Thank you very much.
I thank the representative of Spain for the statement, and I now give the floor to the representative of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela.

Thank you, Mr. President, the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela is grateful for the efforts of Denmark and Pakistan, co-chairs in 2025 of the informal working group on documentation and other procedural issues in preparing this session. We reaffirm that transparency, openness, inclusion, and accountability must guide all the activities approaches and procedures of the Security Council in conformity with the comprehensive compendium set down in note 507 adopted on the 13th of December of 2024. A council that works with clear, predictable methods strengthens the legitimacy of its decisions in the eyes of all the members of the United Nations. As far as penholdership, we reiterate our concern about the use of this mechanism to promote particular agendas at the expense of collective approaches geared towards consensus. We reaffirm that those who are penholders or co-penholders must act responsibly with impartiality and commitment to reliable sources and reiterate the need of a more equitable distribution of this function. including greater participation of elected members, and in particular the three African members, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Liberia, and Somalia, with regard to topics pertaining to their own regions, as well as the elaboration of terms of reference that are clear in terms of pen holdership. On the balance between public and private sessions, we value the fact that in 2025, a vast majority of Security Council meetings was in public format. We encourage that this trend be maintained as a general rule, reserving private consultations for those cases where it is where they're essential to promote a frank and constructive exchange between the Council's members. We also highlight the importance of strengthening the interaction between the Security Council and the Peacebuilding Commission, as envisioned in Note 507 and based on the conclusions of the 2025 review of the peacebuilding architecture, including requests for more specific consultation and interactive informal dialogues prior to visiting missions of the Council. We encourage the development of missions of the Council to visit conflict situations, which has been a practice since its first mission to Cambodia and Vietnam in 1964. These missions must be of a diplomatic character to collect firsthand information and support peace processes, always while strictly respecting the sovereignty of the host country. These missions offer members of the Council the possibility of understanding directly the realities on the ground and maintain contact with local actors. We therefore encourage to restore the-- to use this instrument with greater regularity, including through smaller missions when budgetary limitations require it, to establish an essential mechanism for an informed and effective exercise of the functions of the council in the area of maintaining international peace and security. Lastly, The Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela reiterates that strengthening the methods of work of the Security Council is not an end in itself, but rather a means to consolidate multilateralism, the rule of law, and strict respect for the purposes and principles of the Charter. We once again reiterate our firm commitment to continue contributing in a constructive way so that the Council acts with greater transparency, efficiency, inclusion and accountability without double standards or selective approaches and fulfilling its primary responsibility of maintaining international peace and security. Thank you very much, Mr. President.
I thank the representative of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela. And I now give the floor to the representative of the Philippines. You have the floor, please.

Mr. President, the Philippines thanks both Denmark for convening this important annual debate and Ms. Sharmila Thompson for insightful briefing. The effectiveness of the Security Council depends not only on the decisions it takes, but more importantly on its decision-making processes and the working methods underpinning these processes. The Council's working methods are therefore integral to strengthening the Council's legitimacy, credibility and capacity to discharge its responsibilities under the Charter. We therefore welcome Presidential Note S/2024/507 as a practical framework for making the Council's work more transparent, inclusive, accountable, and effective. The challenge is to ensure its faithful and consistent implementation. Mr. President, in our view, strengthening dialogue and interaction with the wider United Nations membership are key. Member States should have genuine opportunities to contribute to the Council's decision-making processes. Meaningful participation and contribution mean more than the opportunity to address the council in meetings such as this. We therefore welcome the note's emphasis on early engagement and consultation, including close consultations with concerned states, neighboring countries, regional organizations, and other stakeholders as appropriate during the process of drafting the council's products. This should become standard practice. In this regard, as ASEAN Chair this year, we put forth ASEAN's perspective in the Council open debates on maritime security and the rule of law. These engagements demonstrated how regional experience in preventive diplomacy, confidence building international law, and practical cooperation with regional groups can enrich the Council's deliberations. We likewise encourage the consistent use of rules 37 and 39, informal interactive dialogues with the relevant non-members, ARIA formula meetings and open debates among others, so that the views and perspectives of the wider membership can be taken into account on any dispute or situation under the Council's consideration. Council Presidents are also encouraged to continue interactive wrap-up sessions and informal dialogues with the wider membership. Elected members should also continue briefing and engaging their respective regional groups on council issues. We're also concerned by the delay this year in constituting the council's subsidiary bodies. This has affected the participation and engagement of the wider membership of the council. So we support suggestions raised by E10 and the briefer this morning to revisit and strengthen certain sections of the note. On the appointment of the UN Secretary General, we encourage the council to provide the wider membership with public information on the outcome of the straw polls, consistent with the respective roles of the General Assembly and the Security Council in the selection and appointment process, bearing in mind rule 141 of the rules of procedure of the General Assembly. More generally, as principal organs of the United Nations, Ways and means beyond the annual Security Council report should be considered to enhance the relationship between the General Assembly and the Security Council, as is being done between the General Assembly and the ECOSOC. Mr. President, more open, transparent, inclusive, and predictable Council working methods would contribute, in our view, to a more effective Council. By engaging earlier, listening more broadly, and drawing systematically on the perspective of the wider membership, the council can make decisions that would command more ownership and thus lead to more active participation of the general membership in implementing council decisions. In conclusion, the Philippines encourages the faithful implementation of the presidential note S-2024-507 and strengthening the provisions where experience demonstrates such need. Thank you.
I thank the representative of the Philippines for the statement, and I now give the floor to the representative of Guatemala.

Mr. President, Guatemala would like to thank Denmark for convening this annual debate and reiterates its support for a more transparent, inclusive, and effective Security Council. We also thank As my delegation has noted on previous occasions, working methods are not a purely procedural matter. They determine the legitimacy with which this organ exercises the primary responsibility conferred upon it by the Charter, and their impact transcends the Council itself, as it bears on the legitimacy of the United Nations as a whole. For that reason, Guatemala wishes to reiterate four priorities. First, we note with concern the consistent delay in the allocation of chairs of subsidiary bodies, which this year have once again affected the functioning of sanctions committees and working groups. In previous years, the Council has already heard various proposals aimed at improving the process for allocating these chairs. In that regard, we call for continued consideration of these proposals and for the adoption of measures to prevent this situation from recurring. We also recall that Note 507 indicates that Council members are committed to making every effort to agree on the appointment of chairs for the following year no later than the first of October. In that regard, we call for the full and predictable implementation of Note 507. Second, Guatemala considers it essential to continue promoting restraint in the use of the veto. We recognize the value of the mechanism established for the General Assembly to consider situations in which this prerogative is exercised, and renew our call on the permanent members to refrain from using it in situations of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity. Third, Guatemala favors broadening access to penholdership and more equitable distribution in the assignment of the penholder. including co-penholdership arrangements with clear terms of reference, would help strengthen the quality and legitimacy of the Council's decisions. Finally, within the framework of the process for selecting the next Secretary-General, we consider it equally important that this process be conducted with the highest standards of transparency and inclusiveness toward the General Membership. Mr. President, the Security Council's capacity to maintain international peace and security will be strengthened insofar as it acts with transparency, openness, and efficiency, while remaining responsive to the perspectives of the United Nations membership. Guatemala will continue to support, from within the General Membership, every genuine effort aimed at strengthening the implementation and continuing the modernization of the working methods of this Council, as an indispensable step towards a broader and necessary reform of the organ. Thank you.
I thank the representative of Guatemala for the statement, and I now give the floor to the representative of Kenya.

Mr. President, I applaud Denmark's presidency and thank you for convening this important discussion. I would also like to thank Ms. Shamala Thompson for her briefing. Kenya welcomes the continued evolution of the Security Council's working methods and the guidance that note S/2024/507 provides. Having served on the Security Council across three distinct eras, most recently in 2021, 2022, Kenya has witnessed firsthand how changes in the international system have shaped the Council's agenda and working methods. In our experience, effective working methods must adapt to changing realities while strengthening how authority is exercised, consensus built, and the Council's legitimacy and effectiveness sustained. Mr. President, allow me to make five general observations in line with today's debate. First, Note 507 serves as an important compendium of the Council's working methods. However, some provisions are unevenly applied depending on the circumstances, the Presidency or the composition of the Council, thereby impacting on the Council's work. We therefore encourage periodic reviews of the implementation and application of the codified practices to help identify recurring difficulties, capture lessons learned, and recommend practical adjustments to ensure that Note 507 remains responsive to the council's evolving needs. Second, all council members have a voice and a vote, but this does not always translate into equal procedural influence. Asymmetries in access to information, Agenda setting, penholdership, institutional memory and established working practices can constrain the ability of elected members to shape outcomes. To address this, we encourage a more inclusive decision-making process and collective ownership of the council's work. Regional perspectives could, where relevant, be incorporated at an early stage of drafting. on matters with significant regional implications and more opportunities for pen holdership could be afforded to elected members as co-leads on selected files. Third, occasional deadlocks in the selection and appointment of chairs and vice chairs of subsidiary bodies paralyze those institutions. To unlock such deadlocks, we encourage early consultations to ensure timely appointment of the leadership of the subsidiary bodies. We also call for a fair distribution of responsibilities among all Council members. Fourth, Mr. President, Rules 37 and 39 provide important avenues for meaningful participation by non-Council members in this Council's deliberations. Kenya supports the predictable, consistent and purposeful application of the rules and encourages the council to engage regional and sub-regional organizations more systematically, building on the regional perspectives and expertise. The council should make more strategic use of the peacebuilding commission where its engagement can add value to the prevention and sustenance of peace or of the global peace agenda. Fifth, The working methods should help manage rather than deepen political divisions. The Council is currently operating in an increasingly polarized geopolitical environment where existing divisions can sometimes compound political contestations. These situations call for informal approaches such as retreats and consultations to narrow differences and build understanding before positions become entrenched, making disagreement more manageable and consensus more attainable. This approach should guide major processes involving the wider membership, including the selection of the Secretary-General, where transparency, inclusiveness and merit should be pursued with regard to the respective prerogatives of the General Assembly and the Security Council. Mr. President, going forward, we propose that the next phase of discussion focus not only on the standards we've endorsed, but on how consistently those standards are applied, particularly under conditions of political pressure and procedural complexity. Kenya recognizes the urgent need for comprehensive reform of the UN Security Council to make it more effective and representative. We acknowledge the complementary role of the reform of working methods and that structural reform of the Security Council and reaffirm our determination to work together towards this end. Questions of representation, membership and the veto remain essential and must continue to be addressed. We encourage meaningful participation by the wider UN membership in discussions geared towards making the Security Council's working methods more predictable, inclusive, transparent, accountable and adaptive to contemporary realities. I thank you.
Thank you, representative of Kenya, for the statement. And I now give the floor to the representative of Paraguay.

Thank you, Mr. President. First of all, we want to wish you every success in your presidency. Our delegation is grateful for the opportunity to take the floor in this debate, and we would like to congratulate the Danish presidency of the Security Council, because we understand that annual debates on the methods of work of this Council are of extreme importance for the evolution of an efficient collegial body that is capable of fulfilling the mandate and doubt by the charter. This procedural situation in fact underscores the imbalance of power not only between the permanent and non permanent members, but also between members of the Council and the membership generally speaking. Mr. President, the relationship between the General Assembly and the Security Council continues to be a very important aspect. Our delegation considers that this should be strengthened and that the Council should acknowledge that its legitimacy depends on respect of the full membership and the strict compliance with its mandate, is why it should make efforts to become more representative, transparent, effective and responsible vis-a-vis its decisions. The peace and security pillar is under is being examined by the international community, even though it's not a universal body, the work of the Security Council is a global thermometer of the effectiveness of the work of the United Nations in terms of maintaining international peace and security. With this in mind, we welcome the efforts of the informal working group on documentation and other procedural issues for the publication of its annual report guided by the principles of openness, dialogue and inclusion. This should continue. Mr. President, Member States have witnessed great divergences that exist with regard to the use of the veto during the last session of intergovernmental negotiations on the reform of this organ, Paraguay considers that the veto should be abolished, be limited or formally restricted, especially for cases that include measures aimed at preventing the most serious crimes or mass atrocities. Likewise, it's very important to be aware that the use of this right implies great responsibility and ultimately should be used with full responsibility and should lead to accountability in line with the principle of legal equality among all states. Along the same lines, we consider that the members of the United Nations cannot implement the Charter in a selective manner, which is why we urge for the full application of Article 27. The quality of annual reports of the Council are an obligation towards the plenary of the General Assembly, and we believe they should be less descriptive and more in-depth in terms of analysis and and should include analysis of the most delicate decisions that the Council has taken. Finally, Paraguay is in favor of the process of selecting the Secretary General as transparent as possible based on equity. And we also believe that it's very important that the role of the General Assembly is not limited to simply rubber stamping the recommendation of the Security Council. Thank you.
I thank the representative of Paraguay for their statement. And I now give the floor to the representative of El Salvador.

Mr. President, El Salvador is grateful for convening this debate and for your work in promoting ongoing reflection on methods of work of the Security Council. We reaffirm the positions that have been expressed in the past by our delegation in previous debates on the need for a Council that is more transparent, inclusive, representative, and effective. Today, we want to focus on a number of areas where we believe it is necessary to make more concrete progress. First of all, I would like to highlight the relationship between the Security Council and the Peacebuilding Commission. My country has consistently advocated for strengthening the complementarity between both organs and as a current member of the Commission, we reaffirm our commitment to actively contribute to strengthening this relationship. The Commission could offer the Council a preventive perspective, a long-term preventive perspective based on national appropriation and a more in-depth knowledge of the factors that sustain peace. However, for this contribution to have impact, it must take place at time when it can still have an effect on decisions. We also urge the Council or those who exercise drafting functions to systematically solicit the input of the Commission, in particular before renewal of mandates or during transition processes, and to formulate more specific requests that allow the Commission to offer timely and relevant recommendations. Note 507 promotes instruments to achieve this, including informal interactive dialogues with the presidency of the Commission and specific country configurations. Secondly, it's impossible to separate the methods of work from the impact of the veto. El Salvador reiterates our profound concern about its use and the consequences that it continues to have on the capacity of the Council to act in the face of threats to international peace and security. This concern is not limited to the formal veto. The threat, whether explicit or implicit, of its use could also prevent proposals from being submitted, negotiated or subject to voting. In other words, the paralysis of the Council is not always reflected in its voting records. This is why we support continuing to explore measures that limit its use, strengthen transparency regarding its effects, and strengthen existing mechanisms of accountability. With this in mind, we reaffirm our support for resolution 76/262 and the role of the General Assembly when the Council is not capable of acting. We consider that accountability must encompass not only decisions that the Council adopts, but also those that it has not managed to adopt. Thirdly, we want to refer to the function of penholder-ship and co-penholder-ship. The ten elected members represent two-thirds of the membership of the Council and therefore offer regional perspectives, experience and political capability that should make a contribution of substance in elaborating the decisions of the Council. We value the gradual expansion of co-chairmanship arrangements between permanent members and elected these arrangements could combine institutional memory with regional knowledge and contribute to expanding legitimacy and support for the products of the Council. However, penholdership should go further. It requires real responsibilities, early consultations and sufficient time to negotiate and to seek genuine consensus. This responsibility also includes listening to those who will need to implement the decisions adopted, and in particular before renewing or changing peacekeeping mandates, PAM holders or Co-PAM holders should maintain substantive consultations with, in a timely way, troop contributing countries and police contributing countries, and their opinions must be duly considered in elaborating these texts. These consultations cannot simply become a formal exercise. They should make it possible for decisions of the Council to reflect the operational realities on the ground. Fourthly, The process underway, the selection and appointment of the next Secretary General, is concrete proof of the transparency and inclusiveness that we are seeking to strengthen. We value the progress achieved in the participation of membership and we believe it is essential to preserve this through all the phases of this process. Transparency, should not diminish as the process advances toward the Council. There should be a strict close coordination and continued coordination with the General Assembly, predictable rules and equitable access to relevant information for all member states. The future leader of the organization must come from a process that strengthens rather than reduces the confidence of the membership of the United Nations. Lastly, we reiterate that the full, egalitarian and meaningful participation of women must continue to be part and parcel of the methods of work of the Council. This requires not only ensuring their participation as rapporteurs, but also systematically incorporating the analysis on the differentiated impact of conflicts on women and girls in the deliberations and decisions of the Council. Mr. President, The methods of work are not merely a procedural issue. They determine who participates, who can influence a decision, what perspectives are heeded, and ultimately the capacity of the Council to act. El Salvador will continue to contribute to these efforts, convinced that a more inclusive Council and its procedures will be a more legitimate Council and more effective in its decisions. Thank you.
I thank the representative of El Salvador for the statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Belgium.

Mr. President, Excellencies, I have the honor to speak on behalf of the Benelux countries, a longstanding regional partnership compromising Luxembourg, the Kingdom of the Netherlands, and my own country, Belgium. On the outset, we thank the Danish Presidency for having convened this open debate on the working methods of the Security Council. We also wish to sincerely thank the Executive Director of Security Council Report for her briefing and recommendations. The Benelux countries firmly believe that improving the working methods of the Security Council is essential to strengthening its transparency, accountability, inclusiveness and effectiveness. At a time when the credibility of multilateral institutions is at stake, improving working methods is fundamental. We would like to highlight four points. Firstly, we share the concerns voiced by many delegations regarding the current deadlock in the appointment of chairs and vice-chairs of subsidiary bodies. A record delay has severely affected the work of the Council. Delays should not become the norm. We encourage Council members to identify practical solutions and contingency measures. that will ensure the timely allocation of these responsibilities and the uninterrupted functioning of the Council's subsidiary organs. Secondly, on the forthcoming appointment of the next Secretary General, this is of critical importance for the United Nations. The Benelux countries continue to advocate for a fair, transparent and inclusive selection process conducted on an equal basis for all candidates and fully in line with relevant General Assembly resolutions and established good practices. We welcome the public hearings of candidates and the improvement of the preliminary stages of the selection process. However, transparency could be enhanced, in particular, if the Security Council could communicate the results of the straw polls it conducts. More broadly, we see clear merit in further strengthening the relationship between the Security Council and the General Assembly. Enhanced exchanges between these two organs can contribute to greater accountability, transparency, and trust across the membership. The General Assembly's role as the most representative body of the United Nations should be fully reflected in these efforts. Thirdly, according to Article 24 of the Charter, the Security Council acts on behalf of the entire membership of the United Nations. Its working methods should therefore be as transparent and inclusive as possible. We encourage the continued use of mechanisms that facilitate meaningful exchanges with the wider membership, including area formula meetings, direct interactions with stakeholders, NGOs and civil society representatives. These can enrich the Council's understanding of ongoing crises. We also support strengthening interaction between the Security Council, the General Assembly, ECOSOC and the Peacebuilding Commission, as well as ensuring that the Council benefits from relevant expertise across the United Nations system, including from the human rights pillar. And finally, the continued use and threat of use of the veto remains one of the principal obstacles to the Council's ability to fulfill its primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security. The Benelux countries reiterated support for initiatives aimed at promoting restraint in the use of the veto, particularly in situations involving mass atrocities. We also welcome efforts by the General Assembly to enhance accountability following the use of a veto. We further recall the importance of Article 27 of the Charter, which stipulates that a party to a dispute shall abstain from voting. Respect for this provision would strengthen confidence in the impartiality and credibility of the Council. Mr. President, the Benelux countries remain firmly committed to supporting improvements to the working methods of the Security Council. A more transparent, inclusive and effective Council is in the interest of all Member States and essential to the credibility of our multilateral system. I thank you.
Thank you for the statement. And I now give the floor to the representative of Ecuador.

It affects its capacity to fulfill its mandate. difficulties in selecting the chairs and co-chairs of subsidiary bodies is a concrete example of what I'm talking about. I would encourage in particular the E-10 to promote a discussion, a broad and serious discussion on this proposal. When the opacity appears to surround the functioning of this Council, this could increase the feeling of distrust and even of illegitimacy. I thank the representative of Ecuador for the statement, and I now give the floor to the representative of Burundi.

Thank you, President. Thank you for convening this open debate on the Security Council's working methods. This debate is of particular importance at a time when conflicts are multiplying. When humanitarian crises are worsening and where trust in multilateralism is being sorely tested, the credibility of the Security Council depends not only on its capacity to take decisions, but also on the way in which these decisions are drafted, adopted and implemented. Note S/2024/507 is, in this connection, an important tool. It brings together practices and commitments that seek to make the council more transparent, more inclusive, more effective and more efficient. For Burundi, however, the main challenge remains its effective implementation. Working methods only have value if they are applied consistently, predictably and equitably. We should also recognize that there are still some gaps in this. Some practices are not implemented equally. Participation of states directly concerned is not sufficiently predictable. Some procedures don't have clear deadlines and consensus is often hindered by political differences between members of the council. It's on these questions that Burundi would like to focus its intervention. and in doing so we would like to make a few recommendations. Firstly, the Security Council should increase the participation of states directly concerned because decisions are made that have concrete consequences on the people and the states who are not members of the Council. Their voice needs to be heard. Burundi believes that the application of Articles 37 and 39 of the provisional rules of procedure should allow real and substantial participation of States who are directly concerned or particularly affected by the issues on the agenda. Their participation should not be seen as simply a procedural formality. A state that is directly concerned must be able to present its reading of the situation, must be able to explain the realities in the field and share its concerns and contribute to discussions before the Council takes a decision that could affect it. We would therefore propose that when relevant, more clear criteria, more consistent criteria be applied to identify situations where the participation of concerned states is particularly important, all the while fully respecting the prerogatives of the president and the rules of the council. Secondly, we'd recommend making the working methods more inclusive, and this would help reduce divisions within the council. Burundi recognizes the usefulness of the penholder system to allow the council to react swiftly to crises. However, this effect, Effectiveness should also be inclusive. The preparation of texts must be seen as a process allowing for consensus to be found, rather than a process concentrated between a limited number of Members. In this connection, we encourage earlier sharing of draft texts. substantial consultations with all members of the Council, early consultation with the States directly concerned, and better take into account the expertise of regional and sub-regional organisations, and, when necessary, a reasonable time frame allowing for capitals to examine the drafts. We'd also encourage a more systematic use of informal consultations and discussions upstream in order to identify areas of divergence before they become dead ends. The role of a penholder must be one of facilitating consensus, not monopolizing negotiations and how negotiations are led. For Burundi, the transparency of the process for negotiation, early consultation, and the search for common ground are the most effective ways of reducing divisions within the Council. Thirdly, transparency and access to information should be improved. Burundi believes that all Member States must be able to understand, as much as possible, how decisions of the Council are prepared and how they're implemented. We therefore encourage more systematic use of digital tools to facilitate access to Council documentation, particularly for delegations who have more limited capacity. We also encourage the continued publication and regular update of information regarding the Council's working methods. Transparency. doesn't mean that all discussions need to be public, it means that procedures need to be clear, accessible and applied consistently. Burundi also believes that more systematic follow-up of the implementation of note 507 would be useful. Periodic evaluations of council practices would allow progress that's been made to be identified, but it would also identify areas where commitments aren't sufficiently applied. Fourthly, we should also improve the process for appointing chairs and vice chairs of subsidiary bodies. A delay in appointment of them is a particularly worrying issue. These bodies play an essential role in the implementation of Council decisions, particularly on sanctions, counter-terrorism and indeed on the follow-up of some files. When they are delayed in their work, the whole efficiency of the Council is affected. Burundi believes that the procedure set forth in paragraphs 124 to 129 of note 507 should be strengthened further by further transparency and early consultations. The current difficulties seem particularly, would appear to be linked to a lack of sufficiently swift agreement between members of the council and a lack of, and also late consultations and the need to strike an acceptable balance in how responsibilities are distributed. We would therefore encourage the establishment of a more clear calendar sufficiently upstream of appointment and also early consultations between members of the council and also procedure allowing to quickly identify nominations or preferences from members and active the seeking of consensus before disagreements become deadlocks and also distribution of responsibilities that takes into account the capacities, experience and as much as possible equitable representation between different regions. The aim must be to avoid that a procedural issue delays for a long time the functioning of a subsidiary body. Fifth, we should also strengthen relations between the Security Council, the General Assembly and regional organizations. The Security Council acts on behalf of all members of the organization. It should therefore be able to maintain a close dialogue with the entire UN community. Burundi attaches particular importance to the idea of strengthening relations between the Security Council and the General Assembly. We encourage regular discussions between the presidents of the two bodies, as well as a more substantial dialogue, substantive dialogue on issues of common interest. We also believe that cooperation with regional organizations must be strengthened. For Burundi, this is of particular importance because of the strategic relationship between the United Nations and the African Union. Regional organizations often have the historic, political and operational knowledge of the situations that the Council should make the most of, that therefore should make the most of regional expertise. should not only be mobilized once a crisis is already there, it should be included from the very first stages of prevention, mediation and solution seeking. Sixthly, we should also ensure that the work of the Council is closely aligned with the realities in the field. Working methods should allow the Council to better understand the reality that people are facing Burundi continues therefore to support more regular field missions of the Security Council particularly to regions that are directly affected by conflict presence in the field allow members of the Security Council to hear directly from national authorities, regional organizations, affected communities, humanitarian actors and other stakeholders. It could contribute to improving the quality of decisions made and it could also strengthen their ownership. A Council that listens more is a Council that can take better decisions. President, Burundi believes that the reform of the working methods of the Security Council should serve a broader goal. which is to make the Council more representative, more transparent, more inclusive, more effective and more legitimate in the eyes of all Member States. We should, however, recognise one reality. Improving the working methods, as necessary as it may be, cannot alone resolve all the political differences that are affecting the Council. However, it can create the conditions for a more constructive dialogue, for better understanding of the positions of different members, and also it can help find consensus more effectively. In a world that is so profoundly divided, we need a council that is able to reach consensus without renouncing upon its mandate, able to listen without losing its capacity to act and to take decisions without moving even further away from states directly concerned. Multilateralism can only be restored by new, it cannot be only restored by new rules, it must also be restored by confidence, trust, dialogue, inclusion and consistent application of existing rules. To conclude, Burundi reaffirms that it is ready to work with all member states to contribute to the continuous improvement of the Security Council's working methods. A more open Council will be a credible Council. A more inclusive Council will be a more legitimate Council. And a Council that is more effective will be better able to serve international peace and security. Thank you.
I thank the representative of Burundi for their statement. And I now give the floor to the representative of Sierra Leone.

Thank you, Mr. President. I thank Denmark, holding the presidency this month, for convening this open debate on the implementation of note S/2024/507, and express appreciation to Denmark and Pakistan for the concept note for this open debate. I also thank Ms. Shamila Kandeer-Thomson, Executive Director of Security Council Report, for a very insightful briefing. Working methods matter because they determine whether the Council can take the prompt and effective action entrusted to it under Article 24 of the Charter. Acting on behalf of all Member States under Article 24 and in view of Article 25, the Council must ensure that its procedures command confidence across wider membership of the UN. Ser Leone accordingly regards the council's working methods as Central to the legitimacy Effectiveness and accountability of the council note 507 provides a valuable framework it should however remain a living instrument continuously reviewed against actual experience and strengthened wherever gaps may arise Mr. President Africa's position reflected in the African reform model calls for an accessible, accountable, democratic, representative and more effective Council, especially in an enlarged format. We acknowledge the progress achieved thus far, yet more remains to be done. I will thus highlight five areas. implementation must be more systematic and measurable. We support strengthening the informal working group on documentation and other procedural questions and developing concise annual indicators of implementation, gaps and corrective measures. The digital working methods handbook should be kept continuously updated as a transparent repository of praxis and precedent particularly for incoming members. Second, greater inclusion and shared responsibility are essential. Penholdership remains an important source of influence over council outcomes. We welcome the increased use of co-penholderships and encourage broader, more equitable sharing, particularly on issues affecting the regions of elected members. Early consultations and facilitation should resolve differences before they entrench, so that innovative methods serve consensus building rather than workload management. Third, agreeing the chairs and vice-chairs of subsidiary bodies remains a recurring difficulty that requires a durable solution. Paragraphs 124 to 129 of note 507 provide a useful framework, but the unprecedented delays of recent years show that voluntary consultation alone is not enough. Consultation should begin immediately following each council election, supported by a transparent overview of available positions, and guided by equitable geographical distribution and fair burden sharing. The 1 October target should be a firm political deadline. Crucially, we should agree in advance what happens when that deadline is not met. The Council already relies on objective mechanisms to prevent impasse. including the monthly rotation of the presidency in English alphabetical order and the drawing of lots for matters such as order of speakers. Sierra Leone thus proposes a comparable default. Any chairs or vice-chairs left unassigned by the deadline would be allocated by a pre-agreed objective method, such as rotation or the drawing of lots. applied transparently and adjusted only to preserve equitable geographical distribution and relevant expertise. This would ensure that no subsidiary body is left without leadership and remove the incentive to hold the entire package hostage for unrelated concessions. Consensus would remain the rule for establishing any new subsidiary body. the default would govern only the distribution of leadership, with existing chairs continuing in place until successors are agreed. Fourth, Rules 37 and 39 should be applied consistently and predictably. States whose interests are specially affected should have a meaningful opportunity to participate, particularly where Council action bears directly on their security, sovereignty, territorial integrity, or peace process. Rule 39 briefers should be selected for expertise, relevance, and independence, with their full, safe, and meaningful participation assured. Fifth, the Council must deepen engagement with the wider membership, the General Assembly, the Peacebuilding Commission, regional organizations, troop and police contributing countries, and affected states. The selection of the next Secretary-General is an important test. While respecting the prerogatives of the two organs, it should benefit from early substantive engagement and remain guided by merit, competence, integrity, and broad confidence. Mr. President, for Sierra Leone and Africa, these questions carry particular weight. As the continent remains grossly underrepresented in the Council, it has a strong interest in a Council that listens to affected regions, works with regional organizations, and reflects contemporary realities. At a time when confidence in multilateralism is under strain, the Council cannot afford working methods that entrench paralysis. Sierra Leone therefore calls for measurable implementation of Note 507, more equitable penholdership, timely and fair allocation of subsidiary body leadership backed by an objective default mechanism, consistent application of rules 37 and 39, and stronger engagement with the wider membership. I thank you.
Thank the representative of Sierra Leone for the statement. And I now give the floor to the representative of Namibia.

Thank you, Mr. President. Namibia thanks Denmark for convening this important debate on note 507. which contains important provisions aimed at strengthening transparency, inclusivity, accountability, and effectiveness of the Security Council. I also thank Madam Shamala Kandiah-Thomson for her comprehensive briefing. At a time when multilateralism is being tested by escalating conflicts, deepening geopolitical rivalries, and declining trust in multilateral institutions, the working methods of the Security Council must serve as a tool for building consensus and an essential determinant of the Council's legitimacy, credibility, and capacity to discharge its primary responsibility under the Charter of the United Nations in a manner that is representative, transparent, and responsive to contemporary realities. Mr. President, the adoption of Note 507 was an important achievement, yet its value will ultimately be measured not by what it contains, but by how faithful it is implemented. Too often, agreed working methods are applied selectively, while divisions among council members continue to impede timely and decisive action in situations where international community expects leadership. Namibia is particularly concerned that entrenched divisions among Council members continue to undermine its effective action to threats to international peace and security. To bridge these divisions, members of the Council should renew their commitment to genuine dialogue. compromise and the spirit of Article 24 of the Charter, placing the interests of international peace and security above narrow geopolitical considerations. In this context, Namibia joins other delegations in deplored the continued challenges and delays experienced in the appointment of chairs and vice-chairs of the Security Councils subsidiary bodies. The designation of these chairs should remain a technical and practical exercise guided by consensus, fairness and the collective interest of the Council. Consistent with provisions in para 103 and para 104 of note 507, Namibia strongly believes that the Council is most effective when it benefits from the perspectives of all UN member states, regional and sub-regional organizations, especially the African Union, and affected populations to advance principles of regional ownership and collective security that are at the heart of the charter of the United Nations. Mr. President, more inclusive penholdership arrangements can contribute to stronger ownership of Council's products. The relevant provisions should be implemented in a manner that enables Council members, particularly those representing regions directly affected by issues under consideration, to play meaningful roles in drafting and shaping Council outcomes. The relationship between the Security Council and the General Assembly should be viewed as an ongoing and evolving process with both organs continuously exploring innovative ways to further strengthen their interaction in a manner that is mutually reinforcing, contemporary and fully consistent with their respective mandates. Greater interaction between these principal organs can ensure that concerns of the wider membership are adequately reflected in Council deliberations. As I conclude, Mr. President, the legitimacy deficit of the Security Council cannot be fully addressed through procedural reforms alone. While improved working methods can enhance transparency and efficiency, they cannot substitute the comprehensive Security Council reform. The persistent underrepresentation of Africa remains a historic injustice that weakens the legitimacy of the Council. Until such reform is realized, existing working methods must be implemented in a manner that amplifies the voices of underrepresented regions and ensures equitable participation in the Council's decision-making processes. The international community, does not judge the Security Council by the number of contents of documents it adopts. It judges the Council by its ability to prevent conflict, protect vulnerable populations, and respond effectively when peace and security are threatened. The implementation of Note 507 and the continued strengthening of the Council's working methods offer an opportunity to rebuild trust, improve cooperation and enhance the Council's relevance. Let us ensure that transparency is not selective, inclusivity is not symbolic and accountability is not optional. I thank you, Mr. President.

For example, the expansion of the Council, in line with resolution 62575, which was adopted by consensus, and it's laid the foundations for the negotiation for a more representative Council, a more impartial Council, and a more credible one. I thank the representative of Poland for the statement and I now give the floor to the representative of Morocco.

Mr. President, at the outset, my delegation would like to thank Denmark for convening this important debate on the implementation of Security Council Note 507. I'd also like to thank Ms. Candia Thompson, Executive Director of Security Council Report, for her insightful and detailed briefing. Sir President, the Security Council's working methods are critical to the effectiveness of the Security Council and core to its work. The manner the Security Council deliberates is inseparable from the substance of its decisions. Indeed, the Council's working methods are essential tools for strengthening the effectiveness and inclusivity of the Council and ultimately for enabling it to discharge its mandate for the maintenance of international peace and security. With this understanding, my delegation would like to underline the following three points. First, As chair of the Peacebuilding Commission, Morocco welcomes the Council's growing recourse to the PBC's advice. We hope this practice will be further consolidated in full respect of the Commission's advisory mandate and of the cardinal principle of national ownership, a principle that will be at the heart of the PBC's ministerial meeting of 24 September 2026. Second, we must preserve the institutional balance established by the Charter. Article 24 entrusts the Security Council with the primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security, acting on behalf of the entire UN membership. Article 25 gives effect to this responsibility by requiring member states to accept and carry out the Council's decision. Article 12, in turn, safeguards institutional coherence by providing that while the Council is exercising its functions in respect of a dispute or situation, the General Assembly shall refrain from making recommendations on that same matter. These provisions form a coherence architecture. Article 24 establishes the responsibility, Article 25 ensures authority, and Article 12 prevents duplication and fragmentation of decision-making. This is not an institutional formality. It is essential to enabling the United Nations to speak with one voice and to allow the Security Council to fulfill the primary responsibility that the Charter confers upon it. Third, Morocco firmly believes that the Security Council must make fuller and more effective use of the tools placed at its disposal by the Charter for the peaceful settlement of disputes. Prevention must remain at the heart of our collective action. Dialogue, negotiations and mediation are not merely instruments or tools of last resort. They are the core of international peace and security. Their timely use can prevent tensions, escalation, and crisis. This requires a Security Council that is more anticipatory than reactive, capable of identifying emerging tensions, engaging the parties at an early stage, and encouraging them to resolve their differences through dialogue and peaceful means in full accordance with the UN Charter. In conclusion, Mr. Chair, Mr. President, Morocco remains firmly committed to a multilateralism grounded in the Charter and in respect for international law, convinced that the authority of the Council's decisions is nourished by the confidence inspired by the manner in which they are taken. I thank you.
